papers.title: Asymmetric dispersal alters extinction dynamics in a two-patch metapopulation under an Allee effect
papers.abstract: This paper investigates a two-patch metapopulation model with asymmetric dispersal, motivated by the directional transport of organisms between populations by aquatic currents. We consider a system of ordinary differential equations in which dispersal is population-conserving but directionally asymmetric, and each patch is subject to a strong Allee effect: Populations below a critical threshold decline toward extinction, whereas those above the threshold persist and approach their carrying capacities. We analytically prove the convergence of solutions to equilibria, and identify parameter regimes in which positive equilibria necessarily exist. We then numerically explore the one- and two-parameter steady-state bifurcation structures with respect to combinations of asymmetric dispersal rates and the Allee threshold. In particular, for sufficiently high Allee thresholds, we identify broad parameter regions in which the extinction equilibrium is the unique equilibrium of the system. These extinction regions arise from the interplay between asymmetric dispersal and the Allee effect and, notably, are absent in the corresponding population-conserving dispersal model without an Allee effect. Our results demonstrate that, through 'rescue' effects and emergent extinction regimes, directional dispersal can fundamentally help or hinder population persistence in systems subject to the Allee effect, highlighting important implications for the conservation and restoration of endangered species experiencing asymmetric dispersal.

papers.title: Stomatal conductance and net photosynthesis depend on nitrogen supply in drought-limited boreal forest
papers.abstract: Transition from cold limitation to drought limitation due to climate change is widespread in boreal forests. We explored in the scope of the Dry Boreal Forest Long-Term Nitrogen Fertilization Experiment (DryBoreal-LTNE) in southern boreal forests of Mongolia how N supply interacts with tree water and C relations in forests of Larix sibirica, which are naturally drought-limited. Using branches of mature L. sibirica subjected to N fertilization of 6.25-25 kg N ha-1 a-1, we conducted CO2/H2O gas exchange measurements to examine how N availability interferes with the climatic control of stomatal conductance (gs) in L. sibirica. We tested the hypotheses that gs increases with increasing N availability and that this increase can be translated into increased net photosynthesis (A) in L. sibirica even under the dry continental climate of Mongolia. We could confirm the first hypothesis and found that A decreased at low fertilization (6.25 kg N ha-1 a-1) probably caused by increases in respiration due to metabolic costs of intensified N uptake. A attained the highest values at 12.5 kg N ha-1 a-1, but declined at the highest fertilization level of 25 kg N ha-1 a-1. Our results demonstrate that research on the drought tolerance of boreal forests under climate change should not only focus on changes in temperature, vapor pressure deficit, and precipitation, but should take N availability into account, especially as N availability is thought to decrease in remote boreal forests due to elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations and can be locally influenced by land use.

papers.title: Elephant poaching continues in northern Botswana: spatial patterns and policy implications
papers.abstract: Illegal killing for ivory is the primary threat to the endangered African savanna elephant (Loxodonta africana). Botswana has the world's largest elephant population and experienced little poaching during the continent-wide poaching outbreak of the early 2000's. In 2018, however, evidence of widespread elephant poaching in Botswana began to appear, with an estimated 385 elephants poached. Here, we update the status of elephant poaching in northern Botswana with new data collected in 2023-2026. We also used spatial models to determine the factors associated with elephant poaching locations and to better understand poacher behavior. From late 2023 through mid-2026, we located 202 poached elephants in a ~10,000 km2 area of northern Botswana, north and east of the Okavango Delta and mostly west of Chobe National Park. All poached elephants were believed to be adult males. Using point process models, we found that, depending on the method used to locate carcasses, poaching locations were associated with greater distance from roads, higher slope, lower distance to military posts, higher Enhanced Vegetation Index in the dry season, and greater distance from the Namibia border than random points. The poaching outbreak documented in 2018 was not transient: illegal killing for ivory appears to have continued. Because poachers are targeting adult males, their numbers could become depleted in our study area, which has implications for elephant social behavior, legal elephant hunting, and ecotourism. We encourage the government of Botswana to take immediate action against poaching, including improving monitoring and strengthening transboundary cooperation.

papers.title: Effective Fungal SynCom Assembly in Wheat Depends on Field Cooccurrence Patterns
papers.abstract: Plant-associated microbial communities can improve plant resilience to stress and as such are a promising avenue for the future of agricultural technologies to improve crop health. Ideally, synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) are simplified versions of real-world communities that can recapitulate their function. However, SynCom applications often have variable results, we hypothesize is due to the gap between the ideal and realized community. Understanding the mechanisms that support effective SynCom assembly is a key step to unlocking this resource. We investigated how fungal assembly mechanisms (priority, diversity) impacted wheat response to drought. The SynComs contained a single pioneer fungus applied first, followed by low diversity (3 fungi) or high diversity (9 fungi) community inoculations. Plants were then grown under drought or well-watered conditions. We measured plant phenotypic traits and realized fungal community. Realized communities contained a small set of the inoculated SynCom taxa and were not impacted by any treatment. To understand this outcome, we asked if fungal traits or field distributions could predict fungal persistence. We found that persistent SynCom taxa were those that were highly connected hubs in the field network, suggesting that fungi that cooccur and interact with many taxa are more likely to succeed in SynCom applications. Initial and realized SynCom composition influenced plant performance but not in a systematic way. This study highlights the importance of considering natural microbial communities during SynCom design to increase establishment and success of fungal taxa to improve crop stress tolerance.

papers.title: Tree roots drive POM losses and transient MAOM gains across AM and ECM stands
papers.abstract: Roots play a central role in soil organic matter (SOM) formation, stabilization and decomposition, yet how roots and soil properties modulate these dynamics is poorly understood. We used ingrowth cores to investigate how roots influence particulate organic matter (POM) and mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) in forest plots dominated by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) and ectomycorrhizal (EcM) trees in Indiana (IN) and New York (NY), USA. Additionally, we amended a subset of cores with nutrients or water (controls) to examine how nutrient availability affects root-induced changes in POM and MAOM at a moderately N-limited site (IN) and a strongly N-limited site (NY). We tested three hypotheses: H1) root-induced changes in SOM fractions differ between tree-mycorrhizal types, with EcM roots promoting POM losses and AM roots enhancing MAOM gains, H2) increases in nutrient availability reduce POM loss and enhance MAOM formation, with the greatest changes occurring at the most N-limiting environments (NY), and H3) root-induced changes in POM and MAOM fluctuate over time, as initial gains in SOM are offset by SOM losses. We found partial support for H1 and H2 and modest support for H3. For H1, POM-C losses outpaced MAOM gains in EcM-dominated plots (as hypothesized) but both SOM fractions were mostly unchanged in AM-dominated plots. For H2, nitrogen addition did not increase POM-C (as hypothesized), but it did increase MAOM-C modestly in AM plots and EcM plots at the more N-limited (NY). In support of H3, MAOM gains observed after 24 months had generally diminished by 35 months. This was especially true for MAOM-N at the NY site which declined by 13.4%. Together, our results show that roots can simultaneously accelerate losses from POM and promote MAOM accumulation, and that tree-mycorrhizal type, environmental context and time modulate these effects. Additionally, our study suggests that short-term studies of root-SOM interactions may provide an incomplete view of soil C persistence drivers in forests, which can change dynamically over time.

papers.title: Recent trends show a 20 year decline in global biological invasion rates
papers.abstract: Biological invasions are costly economically and environmentally. Despite international agreements to mitigate invasions, we have limited understanding of recent trends - the last two decades of invasion records have been typically excluded from analyses, given potential discovery and reporting lags. We use simulations to show discovery lags do not cause spurious recent declines, but reporting lags can do so. Using global empirical patterns, we estimated reporting lags caused up to a 94% underestimation of recent invasion rates. After controlling for these lags, our model estimated that the invasion rate accelerated at 1.5%/yr between 1970 and 2003 up to a maximum of ~650 species/yr, but has since declined to ~150 species/yr in 2020. Thus, for global trends, our analyses indicate that observed empirical declines are likely real and that lags cannot explain them, potentially suggesting that invasion policies have been effective.

papers.title: Bacterial community patterns of the Antarctic stalked jellyfish Haliclystus antarcticus and antimicrobial activity from a gut-associated Oceanisphaera ostreae isolate
papers.abstract: Host-associated microbiomes are increasingly recognized as important components of cnidarian biology, yet their diversity and organization remain poorly understood in non-coral lineages, particularly in polar environments. Staurozoans, or stalked jellyfishes, are a small and understudied group of benthic medusozoans whose associated bacterial communities remain largely unexplored. Here, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to characterize bacterial communities associated with the Antarctic stalked jellyfish Haliclystus antarcticus collected from two coastal sites in the South Shetland Islands, Byers Bay and Risopatron. We examined three anatomical compartments (gut, peduncle, and tentacles) to investigate patterns of bacterial community diversity and composition. Gut samples exhibited the greatest variability in richness-based alpha diversity, whereas peduncle and tentacle samples displayed more constrained diversity profiles. Across compartments, 47 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were shared, indicating a recurrent bacterial component within the host-associated communities. Gut samples exhibited the strongest differential-abundance signal, while genera such as Polaribacter and Planktotalea were identified as indicators of tentacle-associated communities. In parallel, we isolated and characterized a gut-associated bacterium identified as Oceanisphaera ostreae. Genomic and metabolomic analyses revealed diverse biosynthetic potential and multiple metabolite-related features. Preliminary bioactivity screening indicated antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus, with no cytotoxicity detected against HCT-116 cells under the tested conditions. Together, these results provide the first characterization of the H. antarcticus microbiome, demonstrating anatomical and geographic variation in bacterial communities and identifying a cultivable bacterial associate with potentially relevant metabolic capabilities.

papers.title: Winter agricultural practices matter : rice stubble cover and landscape feature diversity increase abundance of wintering farmland birds in the Camargue
papers.abstract: Agricultural intensification has led to a decline of farmland bird populations worldwide. Most studies have focused on the role of practices on birds during the breeding season but little is known about the role of practices during winter. Here, we study the effect of different types of winter field cover and landscape features on wintering birds in the rice production area of the Camargue (Rhone delta, France). We conducted bird surveys in 86 organic crop fields during winter. We hypothesized that the type of field cover (rice stubble, bare ground, winter wheat, grasslands), and the type of landscape features (hedegrows, grass strips and reed strips) have an effect on the abundance and species richness of wintering bird communities at field level. Moreover, we hypothesized that the diversity of field cover types and landscape features at the landscape level have a positive effect on the abundance and species richness of wintering bird communities, in line with the landscape complementation hypothesis. Results show that at the field level, rice stubble fields accommodate higher bird abundance that fields with other cover types. Moreover, we show that this pattern is driven by a few gregarious and granivorous wintering species while others preferred grasslands. At the landscape level, we show that the diversity of landscape features increased wintering bird abundance. We also show species-specific responses to different types of landscape features with hedgerows, reed strips and grass strips affecting diverse species at both field and landscape levels. Overall, our results suggest that rice stubble provide important winter habitats for declining granivorous species, while maintaining a heterogeneous mosaic of landscape features benefits wintering bird communities. Finally, we quantify species-specific response to the surface of different landscape features, a key step to build-up dedicated agri-environmental schemes.

papers.title: Iterative prioritisation of upstream and downstream passage remediation for the critically endangered European eel (Anguilla anguilla) at pumping stations
papers.abstract: The European eel (Anguilla anguilla) is critically endangered and subject to regulations requiring safe passage at migratory barriers and water intakes, but remediation must be prioritised to maximise conservation benefits. This study developed a novel prioritisation framework for both upstream and downstream eel passage remediation in heavily modified and fragmented pumped river systems. Catchment area (habitat quantity), distance from the tidal limit and numbers of migration barriers downstream were used as baseline geospatial metrics for bi-directional passage data. Following this, eel presence/absence data was incorporated to separate sites into upstream and downstream passage prioritisations, with site-specific hydrological connectivity (downstream) and fish community richness (upstream) data further refining rankings. Prioritisation rankings were compared iteratively to assess the influence of combining variables. Eel presence/absence data substantially altered downstream passage priorities relative to geospatial metrics alone, with a maximum rank change of 96 and eleven sites changing by 50 or more places. For downstream passage, hydrological connectivity resulted in significant re-ranking of priorities. For upstream passage, including fish species richness as an indicator for habitat quality caused notable re-ranking of sites compared with geospatial metrics alone. The results demonstrate that prioritisation based solely on geospatial metrics risks overlooking important sites and, consequently, directing resources towards areas with limited conservation potential. The iterative, flexible framework presented in this study provides a transparent and transferable approach for informing eel passage investment within heavily modified drainage systems and could be adapted to other landscapes where anguillid eels are conservation priorities.

papers.title: Tracing urban diet shifts into guppy stoichiometry in Trinidadian streams
papers.abstract: Urbanization can alter dietary stoichiometry by changing the elemental composition of food resources or the mixture of resources consumers assimilate. However, the relative contributions of resource elemental quality and assimilated diet composition to dietary stoichiometry, and whether the resulting dietary differences are reflected in consumer body stoichiometry, remain poorly understood, particularly in omnivores. We sampled adult female Trinidadian guppies (Poecilia reticulata) and their food resources from paired high-urbanization (HU) and low-urbanization (LU) sites in three rivers of Trinidad's Northern Range. Combining hierarchical Bayesian stable-isotope mixing models with resource %C, %N, and %P, we reconstructed dietary stoichiometry, partitioned differences between urbanization levels into contributions from diet composition and resource elemental quality, and compared these with somatic stoichiometry. Under the primary mixing model, aquatic invertebrates contributed less to estimated HU diets (33.7 percentage points lower; 95% credible interval [5.0, 60.1]), whereas detrital contributions tended to be higher. Resource elemental composition showed no consistent differences between urbanization levels. Under this model, reconstructed dietary N:P ratios were lower in HU guppies (by 59.2% [10.0, 81.8]), while C:N ratios tended to be higher, and C:P ratios tended to be lower. Changes in assimilated source mixtures contributed more strongly than resource elemental quality to C:N and N:P differences. All of these contrasts depended on the estimated trophic discrimination factors, weakening under fixed literature values, with the C:N contrast reversing under two of them and the detrital contrast varying in direction. Guppy somatic tissues partly tracked these dietary differences. HU guppies tended to have lower somatic C:P and N:P ratios, in the same direction as their diets but of smaller magnitude. Somatic C:N showed no clear difference, and the dietary C:N contrast was itself uncertain. Our findings suggest that urbanization reshapes guppy dietary stoichiometry mainly through shifts in which resources they assimilate, and that guppies only partially pass these shifts into their bodies. Understanding the stoichiometric consequences of environmental change therefore requires considering not only what resources contain, but also which resources consumers assimilate.

papers.title: Can a woody encroaching species affect woodlands? Impacts of eastern redcedar (Juniperus virginiana) overdominance on woodland understories and management scenarios
papers.abstract: Eastern redcedar (Juniperus virginiana L., Cupressaceae; ERC) is rapidly expanding throughout the Great Plains. However, its effects on woodlands, particularly in the Northern Great Plains, are poorly understood, even as managers invest substantially in its removal. To fill this gap, along an ERC dominance gradient in a forest inventory plot in Nebraska, we assessed: (1) how woodland understory plant communities and environmental conditions varied and (2) where and how ERC management had the greatest benefits. Spatial neighborhood analyses showed that greater ERC canopy reduced woody seedling abundance, species richness, and species diversity relative other canopy species. No canopy species, including ERC, was associated with variation in herbaceous species richness. ERC dominance was unrelated to soil moisture, pH, or organic matter, but was associated with reduced understory light, suggesting that dense ERC foliage limits seedling establishment. Simulated management scenarios predicted that continued encroachment would shift the woody understory community toward disturbance-tolerant shrubs and away from canopy tree species, likely altering forest structural and species diversity and reducing habitat quality. ERC removal at low to moderate encroachment levels and from steep canyon habitats was associated with the greatest increases in seedling abundance and species richness, but also small declines in diversity, with implications for the complex decisions of when, where, and how much of this native species to remove. Our results indicate that ERC encroachment has reduced woody species diversity, and left unchecked, will likely continue to do so, with potentially cascading effects on higher trophic levels, biotic interactions, and ecosystem services.

papers.title: Historical overestimated abundance of a Critically Endangered species: the case of the tamaraw (Bubalus mindorensis) of Mindoro Island
papers.abstract: Population abundance is a central parameter in conservation, for which biased estimates can seriously undermine management strategies for threatened species. The tamaraw (Bubalus mindorensis) is a Critically Endangered large herbivore endemic to Mindoro Island, Philippines. The species has been monitored annually at Mounts Iglit-Baco Natural Park (MIBNP) since 2000 using a multi-vantage-point count method that is prone to both imperfect detection and repeated counting of the same individuals across sessions. Because the historical abundance estimation is an index of relative abundance with no probabilistic modeling of counts, the actual number of tamaraw in what is considered as the largest remaining population is still poorly known. To fill this gap, we conducted an independent double-observer experiment over five years (2022-2026) and fitted Bayesian hierarchical detection models to the counts. As expected, detection probability was <1 throughout (single-observer estimates 0.41-0.84; combined-observer 0.68-0.96), confirming that a substantial fraction of animals is missed by rangers during all counts. Compared with these estimates, historical counts overestimated tamaraw abundance by a factor of 1.61-2.34, yielding a mean population size across 2022-2026 of 203 individuals (95% credible interval 182-226) rather than the roughly 400-500 individuals previously assumed. Our results imply that the MIBNP tamaraw population, while more vulnerable to demographic and genetic risks than previously believed, has likely responded positively to ongoing conservation efforts; we recommend that population viability assessments and translocation plans for the species be revised accordingly.

papers.title: Apple floral attractants function across the 24-hour cycle to support potential diurnal and nocturnal pollinators
papers.abstract: Pollination in apple (Malus domestica Borkh.) is typically attributed to diurnal bees, yet nocturnal insects also contribute to fruit set. To assess whether apple flowers recruit potential pollinators throughout the 24-hour cycle, we quantified diel patterns in floral attractants and insect visitation in an orchard in Northwest Arkansas, United States. We measured nectar and volatiles and used a combination of visual surveys, light traps, and video recordings to assess insect abundance and floral visitation while controlling for weather conditions. We found that nectar volume remained consistent across sampling times, indicating that reward availability is dielly stable. Floral volatile bouquets, in contrast, exhibited subtle but significant diel and interannual variation, driven largely by shifts in aldehydes, alkanes, and benzenoids. Several compounds associated with nocturnal moth and dipteran attraction - including alpha-farnesene, benzyl alcohol, and aldehydes - were enriched at night. Apple flowers were visited by insects around the clock. Nighttime visitors were less abundant than daytime visitors but taxonomically diverse, including moths and nematoceran flies, whereas bees, wasps, and brachyceran flies were restricted to daytime. Different taxonomic groups therefore alternated over the diel cycle, producing pronounced shifts in visitor community composition. Thus, apple flowers produce attractants across the diel cycle and nocturnal insects - particularly dipterans and moths - are a consistent, ecologically meaningful component of the apple flower-visiting assemblage. Our findings support the need for pollinator-inclusive management that accounts for the full diel cycle, particularly when scheduling pesticide applications near bloom, to sustain diverse pollinator communities and enhance the resilience of apple production systems.

papers.title: The use of cultured symbionts enhances the survival of reef-deployed coral recruits
papers.abstract: Introduction: Symbiodiniaceae dinoflagellates are essential for coral juvenile development and survival, yet early-life symbiont provisioning remains underused in coral restoration. Objectives: We tested whether inoculating sexually propagated Acropora spathulata recruits with cultured symbionts before reef deployment improves survival and shapes symbiont community composition. Methods: Recruits inoculated with cultured Cladocopium sp. (C1) or Durusdinium trenchii (D1), and uninoculated recruits (Control) were deployed on the central Great Barrier Reef. Results: Both inoculation treatments approximately doubled survival relative to Control, although the benefit varied with local benthic habitat. C1 and D1 recruits were dominated by symbiont sequences matching their respective inoculated cultures, while Control recruits predominantly harboured a Durusdinium-dominant community closely resembling the cultured D1. Cultured C1 was also dominant among most C1-inoculated recruits after nine months, although some diverged from the inoculated community towards a mixed assemblage with Durusdinium. Conclusions: Similar survival benefits in the two inoculation treatments suggest that the timing and success of symbiont establishment were more critical for early survival than symbiont genus identity, under the conditions and period of this study.

papers.title: Species turnover dominates plant trait variation along continental climate gradients
papers.abstract: Variation in plant functional traits along climate gradients chiefly arises from two processes: turnover of species with different trait values, and trait adjustment within species across environments. Yet, the relative contributions of these processes remain poorly quantified, limiting our ability to predict how traits, species distributions and, in turn, ecosystem properties will respond to climate change. Across seven functional traits and 1867 plant taxa from continental Australia, we provide a unified assessment of among- versus within-species contributions across multiple dimensions of plant function. Species turnover emerged as the dominant process driving trait variation along both precipitation and temperature gradients. Nevertheless, the contribution of within-species adjustment to climate differed substantially among traits and was generally greater in non-woody than woody taxa, these patterns being most clearly expressed along precipitation gradients. Our findings imply that plant traits will track changing climatic conditions primarily through species replacement, particularly for traits such as wood density and seed mass. Species may also respond in situ through adjustments in leaf physiology and morphology and, in woody taxa, through shifts in relative allocation between leaves and stem tissues. This knowledge has potential to improve predictions of the structure and function of future plant communities.

papers.title: Differential population declines across migratory strategies are shifting European bird communities towards residency
papers.abstract: Previous studies revealed steep declines in populations of common migratory birds across Europe, especially for long-distance migrants. However, these studies focussed on continental-scale patterns, and they assigned a single migratory strategy to each species, often not distinguishing short-distance migrants from residents. It thus remains unclear whether the same patterns are found across European countries, and whether they hold when taking into account the variation in migratory behaviour observed across the European populations of many species. Here, we examine how European breeding landbird communities have varied according to migratory strategy between 1990 and 2023, at both continental and national scales. By compiling multiple sources of information on seasonal movements, we characterise the migratory strategy of landbird populations per country (long-distance migrant, short-distance migrant or resident). We combined these data with estimates of population trends and of abundance from national monitoring schemes to quantify changes in both multi-species indices (average change across species) and total abundance of birds, for each migratory strategy. At the continental scale, multi-species indices reveal a strong decline in long-distance migrants (-26.8% between 1990 and 2023), whereas short-distance migrants declined more slowly (-4.5%) and residents remained stable. Changes in total abundance show even steeper declines - of 29.9% and 10.2% for, respectively, long- and short-distance migrants - whereas residents increased slightly (+3.4%). Together, these results point to a gradual reorganisation of bird communities towards a greater dominance of resident birds across Europe. However, these changes are not happening homogenously across the continent: whereas in Central and Southern Europe we observed the same general pattern of declining migrants while residents remained broadly stable or increased, in Northern Europe we reveal declines for all migratory strategies. Overall, our study highlights the widespread vulnerability of migratory birds in Europe, while showing that the reorganisation of bird communities follows different trajectories across regions.

papers.title: Normalised whole-plant water supply declines with plant height across the seed-plant phylogeny
papers.abstract: Whole-plant water-transport capacity largely controls terrestrial water fluxes, yet it is unresolved to what extent its variation across the seed-plant phylogeny is structured by shared ancestry, edaphoclimatic conditions, plant height or water relation traits. We fitted a phylogenetic structural equation model to maximum leaf-specific whole-plant hydraulic conductance (kL), together with concurrent Huber value (Hv), stomatal conductance (gs), and height for 263 species spanning the global climate space, partitioning direct from indirect effects, and phylogenetically conserved from independent effects. kL declined with height, and Hv did not offset this decline. Hv raised kL but was unrelated to height among species. kL was lower in wetter niches, despite higher Hv there, indicating lower conductance per unit sapwood area. kL was tightly coupled to gs in both conserved and independent variation, so the height-driven decline in kL propagated to gas exchange. Plant height therefore constrains whole-plant hydraulic supply and, through it, gs.

papers.title: Resistance evolution in a single species reorganizes community responses across a resource-antibiotic landscape
papers.abstract: Rapid evolution in one species can restructure ecological communities, but how its effects vary across environmental conditions remains poorly understood. Here we mapped the consequences of antibiotic resistance evolution in Aeromonas caviae across 64 combinations of resource availability and antibiotic stress in three- and 16-species bacterial communities. Resistance evolution changed where community-state boundaries were located, with boundaries lost or gained depending on resource availability. The same evolutionary change increased diversity in some environments but decreased it in others. Species success was partly explained by growth traits at zero or low antibiotic concentrations and by intrinsic resistance at inhibitory concentrations. Resistance evolution reversed dominance between the two dominant species and changed which traits mattered. It also altered other species' responses below inhibitory concentrations, mostly between closely related species. Our findings show that the consequences of evolution depend on environmental context but can be partly explained by species traits.

papers.title: Forecasting sockeye salmon migration timing and mortality under thermal stress
papers.abstract: Pacific salmon hold high ecological, cultural, and economical importance, but climate change is constraining their survival and reproductive success. Warming rivers are one of the foremost threats, with many populations increasingly facing temperatures approaching or exceeding their physiological limits. Understanding and predicting these negative impacts can inform mitigation or offsetting measures. We used a 12-year dataset of 13801 individually-tagged fish to develop a detailed model of Okanagan sockeye salmon migration based on functional relationships with river temperature and flow. Okanagan sockeye are the largest of the last two self-sustaining sockeye populations in the Columbia River basin. Their abundance increased dramatically over the last two decades amid significant rehabilitation efforts. However, Okanagan sockeye migrate into one of the species' warmest inhabited regions in North America and are highly vulnerable to climate change. Our model revealed temperature thresholds associated with migration cessation and mortality near 21{degrees}C and 25{degrees}C, respectively. These temperatures are common during the migration period in the Okanogan River, which sockeye must ascend to reach the spawning grounds. We used the estimated functional relationships to parameterize forward simulations of Okanagan sockeye migration from 2006-2025, spanning all years where water and fish passage data were available. These simulations accurately predicted migration timing and survival through the Okanogan River, providing a forecasting tool for Canadian fishery managers to regulate harvest in Osoyoos Lake. The simulations also showed elevated mortality rates during warm years and highlighted the perils associated with brief periods of river cooling, which apparently trigger large influxes of salmon migrants who may subsequently be exposed to extreme temperatures and experience high mortality rates. Our work highlights the potential for functional models to provide detailed and accurate reconstructions and forecasts of Pacific salmon migration success, which managers will require as river temperatures increasingly exceed salmon physiological limits.

papers.title: Pollinator response diversity and turnover buffer pollination networks from habitat loss in human-modified landscapes
papers.abstract: Agricultural intensification and habitat fragmentation are major drivers of biodiversity loss, yet their effects on ecological interaction networks remain elusive. In plant-pollinator systems, many species disappear with habitat transformation, but network responses remain inconsistent across studies. We hypothesize that this mismatch arises because local observations often overlook the response diversity of the regional species pools. To test this, we compared observed plant-pollinator networks along a land-use gradient with expectations under hypothetical closed-community simulations. Using data from 30 sites in the Donana Protected Area (southern Spain), we found that spatially connected communities maintained a stable network structure despite habitat loss. This stability was driven by pollinator response diversity, leading to marked species turnover across sites. In contrast, simulated closed communities showed reduced buffering capacity and predominantly negative trends in network metrics such as pollinator richness, total visits, and plant link density. Our results indicate that network stability can emerge from spatial connectivity rather than purely local processes.

papers.title: ADTSIM2.0: An updated simulation of American dog tick (Dermacentor variabilis Acari: Ixodidae) population dynamics
papers.abstract: The American dog tick, Dermacentor variabilis (Say), is found across most of the central and eastern portions of North America, and is a known vector of human and veterinary pathogens. While this tick has been found throughout this region for decades, there is still little understanding of the drivers for the highly variable annual densities. To explore the relative effects of hosts, environmental conditions, and tick biology, we introduce ADTSIM 2.0, an upgraded version of the ADTSIM model that simulates the lifecycle of D. variabilis. The model uses a weekly time step and follows the life stages (egg, larvae, nymph, and adult), questing behavior, host-seeking dynamics, and survival rates under varying environmental conditions. The model includes calculations for tick interactions with small- and medium-sized mammal hosts and factors in critical environmental influences such as temperature on tick development and questing activity. It addresses the effect of questing behavior on tick longevity, emphasizing the trade off between survival and host-seeking. The results show that accurate estimates of both host densities and weather information are critical to predict local D. variabilis densities. This model provides the first step to building a tool for public health information, offering a framework for assessing tick control measures and is adaptable to add tick-borne pathogen dynamics for both human and animal diseases.

papers.title: Biotic interactions buffer the effects of biodiversity loss on ecosystem functioning
papers.abstract: Biodiversity loss generally impairs functions on which nature and societies depend upon. Yet, it is difficult to predict under which conditions losing biodiversity has larger effects on functions such as primary production or carbon retention. We present a theory that demonstrates that biotic interactions mediate the intensity of these effects. In species interaction networks with many or strong trophic links, biodiversity loss has weaker effects on functioning because alternative interaction pathways allow surviving species to compensate for species loss. In contrast, in networks with fewer or weaker links, ecosystem functioning is very sensitive to the extinction of species. Here, we identify interaction erosion as a hidden dimension of the biodiversity crisis that provides a unifying explanation for functional consequences of biodiversity loss across ecological contexts.

papers.title: Complementary roles among traits in community assembly processes of benthic foraminifera
papers.abstract: Organismal traits play a distinct role in shaping community assembly, yet they have received comparatively little attention in marine communities. Here, we focus on living benthic foraminifera, a diverse group of marine protists that inhabit the seafloor. Benthic foraminifera are protists that have evolved different test-construction strategies: either by selecting and agglutinating grains from their surrounding environment or by biomineralization. In addition, taxa exhibit distinct morphologies have been hypothesized to reflect microhabitat partitioning within sediments. Here, we investigate their metacommunity patterns by analysing a co-occurrence network covering the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. We found that test-construction strategies significantly explained the structure of the network, whereas the general test shape did not. We hypothesize that test-construction strategy act as a broader-scale filter on the regional species pool, whereas morphological differences may be more closely related to local-scale coexistence and habitat partitioning. This study supports the idea that different organismal traits have different roles in the community assembly process.

papers.title: Individual symbiont strains can compensate for complex microbiome loss in the bull-headed dung beetle, Onthophagus taurus
papers.abstract: Many animals and plants have evolved to rely on microbiome mediated interactions with their environment. Across diverse insect groups, many are incapable of either breaking down complex carbohydrates or synthesizing essential nutrients despite consuming diets which should require one, or both, functions. Onthophagus beetles are one such host, with recent work suggesting their ability to digest their dung diet, typically rich in tough to digest polysaccharides and poor in nutrients, is likely bolstered by heritable symbionts. Despite there being over 2,000 species of Onthophagus, and over 5,000 species of "true" dung beetles (Scarabaeinae), little is known about how the microbiomes of these beetles modulate their interactions with their dung diet. The work presented here assesses the possible significance of four individual microbiome members, present during Onthophagus taurus development. Results show that three of the four isolates tested partially recovered normative developmental outcomes in O. taurus. Specifically, inoculation with a strain of either Acinetobacter, Brucella, or Pseudomonas increased pupal size relative to beetles deprived of the maternal inoculate. This mirrors the effects of individuals receiving the full natural inoculate, which contains hundreds of bacterial species. Further, using whole genome sequencing, we form a hypothesis of what nutrients these isolates provide to benefit O. taurus development. The findings presented here further highlight Onthophagus dung beetles as powerful systems to study the complex ways in which microbiome function can interact with diet to influence developmental and evolutionary outcomes.

papers.title: Phenotypic plasticity reshapes the evolution of species coexistence
papers.abstract: Modern coexistence theory (MCT) has been the mainstay of recent research on coexistence of competing species. Competition not only drives evolutionary changes in traits that affect coexistence, but also induces rapid plastic changes. However, a generalised framework that integrates plasticity and evolution into MCT is lacking. We formulate such a framework for a system of two competing species and analyse how breadth of available resources modulates the effect of competition-induced plasticity on the evolution of coexistence components (niche and fitness difference). We find that, in broad environments, divergent plasticity accelerates evolution towards positive invasion growth rates for both species, facilitating coexistence, whereas convergent plasticity hinders this process. Surprisingly, in narrower environments, divergent plasticity can hinder coexistence, leading to exclusion, whereas convergent plasticity can facilitate coexistence. Our results show that plasticity reshapes the eco-evolutionary trajectories to coexistence, highlighting the importance of integrating short-term plastic responses with long-term evolutionary dynamics.

papers.title: From individual movement to ecosystem response: how landscape structure shapes herbivore impacts
papers.abstract: Understanding how local interactions generate large-scale ecological dynamics is a central challenge in ecology. In heterogeneous environments, consumer movement links resource distribution with exploitation, producing responses that may not be predicted from consumer abundance or resource availability alone. Here, we develop a spatially explicit stochastic individual-based model of two herbivore populations with contrasting movement and foraging strategies that share renewable resources. The model incorporates heterogeneous resources, consumer movement and feeding, resource regeneration, predation, and refuge availability. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we examine how herbivore pressure and landscape structure shape population dynamics and resource depletion. Movement strongly determines the spatial pattern of depletion, while resource vulnerability depends on the overlap between resource distribution and consumer activity. Counterintuitively, increasing the extent of a productive region increases initial resource biomass but can also increase relative resource loss. Additional resources sustain consumer activity where herbivores concentrate, showing that greater resource availability does not necessarily buffer ecosystems against herbivory. Resource biomass can also decline substantially before major reductions in vegetation occupancy become apparent. These results demonstrate how individual behaviour and landscape structure jointly shape ecosystem responses. The model provides a framework for investigating how spatially coupled consumer-resource interactions generate ecological dynamics.

papers.title: HiFi long-read metagenomics reshapes genome-resolved interpretations of activated sludge microbiome
papers.abstract: Genome-resolved metagenomics is widely used to characterize activated sludge microbiomes and infer the microbial processes underpinning system performance. However, the reliability of metabolic inferences drawn from fragmented short-read (SR) genomes remains insufficiently examined. Using (near-)complete genomes reconstructed from HiFi long-read (LR) sequencing as references, we traced genome recovery through SR assembly and post-assembly processing. Assembly fragmentation and subsequent sequence loss during post-assembly processing compromised the recovery of high-quality genomes despite adequate sequencing depth and breadth of coverage. This incomplete recovery biased inferences regarding denitrification modularity, underestimating complete denitrifier populations and distorting the inferred balance between N2O producers and reducers. Poor recovery of nitrifier and Ca. Accumulibacter genomes, exacerbated by population microdiversity and structurally complex genomic regions, precluded reliable inferences regarding nitrification and phosphorus accumulation. Our findings caution against uncritical interpretation of SR-based microbiome-function linkages and highlight the value of incorporating HiFi LR sequencing into genome-resolved metagenomic analyses.

papers.title: Behavioural response diversity of individual seabirds can correlate positively with colony stability
papers.abstract: Ensuring ecosystems are stable has become a priority given humanity's dependence on the services those ecosystems provide. There has consequently been significant research effort demonstrating that ecosystem stability is driven by 'response diversity', whereby different species respond uniquely to the environmental conditions and 'insure' the ecosystem against collapse. However, response diversity theory has only been applied at the ecosystem/community level, when the response diversity of individual animals' behaviour or traits is also theoretically linked to population-level stability. Therefore, we may be overlooking a viable indicator of extinction risk. Using long-term behavioral and energetic expenditure data from two seabird species breeding in the North Atlantic (Atlantic puffin Fratercula arctica and black-legged kittiwake Rissa tridactyla), we demonstrate that the response diversity in foraging effort of individual birds correlates with the stability of their colony's population size, while energetic expenditure does not. Further, the diversity of bird responses increases when environmental conditions (here represented by sea surface temperature) are outside of the colony's norm. Our work shows that response diversity provides a new perspective on the role of individual behavioral differences in creating stable populations, offering insights to better manage vulnerable groups.

papers.title: Long-read metagenomics reveals unexplored viral diversity andgenomic novelty in the mesopelagic Andaman Sea
papers.abstract: The mesopelagic zone (200 to 1000 m) of the ocean represents Earth's largest yet most underexplored biome, particularly with respect to viral diversity and function. The deep-sea virome of the Indian Ocean remains largely unexplored despite the ecological significance of marine viruses in regulating microbial mortality, biogeochemical cycling and carbon flux via the viral shunt. In this study, we explored the diversity of DNA viruses across mesopelagic depths in the Andaman Sea. Seawater samples collected from multiple depths were enriched for viral particles, followed by viral DNA extraction and long-read metagenomic sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies. We used three complementary approaches for the identification of assembled contigs of viruses. Based on the consensus from these three approaches followed by quality assessment, we retained 1,604 viral contigs of high-confidence and high-quality. Among the taxonomically assigned viruses, members of the class Caudoviricetes dominated across all samples. The assignment decreased substantially at lower taxonomic ranks, highlighting the limited representation of environmental viruses in existing reference databases. Gene-sharing network analysis further revealed genomic novelty and showing limited gene-sharing relationships with reference genomes. Host prediction analyses assigned putative hosts to 10.7% of viral contigs, of which 98.3% were associated with bacteria and 1.7% with archaea. Among predicted bacterial hosts, Pseudomonadota predominated. Structure-informed functional annotation of complete viral contigs identified predominantly structural and tail-associated proteins, while a substantial proportion of viral proteins remained functionally uncharacterized. Collectively, these findings reveal previously under-explored viral diversity in the mesopelagic Andaman Sea study and provide the first comprehensive insight into the deep-ocean virome of this region.

papers.title: Adaptation of Mimulus cardinalis to drought through changes in stomatal conductance
papers.abstract: Many areas around the globe are experiencing warmer temperatures, more extreme drought, and wildfires because of climate change. Therefore, plant populations may experience strong natural selection on traits associated with adaptation to rapid change. One trait likely under selection is stomatal conductance, which determines the rate at which water vapor and carbon dioxide diffuse through the stomata and is sensitive to environmental factors such as drought, CO2, and vapor pressure deficit. The purpose of this study is to understand how plants respond both ecologically and evolutionarily to an extreme multiyear drought. Using six populations of a perennial herb (Mimulus cardinalis), we measured the evolution of operational stomatal conductance in pre-drought ancestral and post-drought descendant cohorts planted in three common gardens across the species' range. This design allowed us to test (1) whether stomatal conductance evolved in response to drought and (2) whether populations with greater genetic variance evolved more. Patterns consistent with drought escape were more common than patterns consistent with avoidance (6 versus 4 of 18 population-by-garden combinations), but evidence for evolutionary change in stomatal conductance was limited overall, and the extent of change was not correlated with genetic variance. These findings offer a framework for future research on stomatal traits and insight into the rate at which plants respond to environmental change.
